US consumers are extremely bullish on stocks:

The perceived probability among US consumers that US stock prices will be higher 1-year from now increased +0.5 percentage points in July, to 41.4%, the highest since April 2021.

Since March, this percentage has risen +5.1 points, marking the 2nd-highest reading since the 2020 pandemic.

By comparison, the April 2020 peak was 51.8%.

By age, consumers under 40 are the most optimistic, at 42.0%, the 2nd-highest since September 2024.

This is followed by the 40-59 age group, at 41.5%, the highest since January 2025, and consumers over 59, at 41.1%, the highest since September 2025.

Bullish sentiment is spreading across all consumer age groups.

The US job market is losing workers at an alarming pace:

The US labor force participation rate fell -0.1 percentage point in July, to 61.4%, the lowest since May 2020.

This metric measures the proportion of working-age Americans either employed or actively looking for work.

Excluding the 2020 pandemic, this is the lowest reading since March 1976.

The decrease also marks the 7th monthly decline over the last 8 months, bringing the cumulative drop to -1.1 percentage points.

This comes as -264,000 people left the labor force in July, following June's -720,000 decline, the 2nd-largest monthly decline since 2020.

Since November, the US labor force has shrunk by more than -2.4 million workers.

The US job market is much weaker under the surface than the headline data suggests.

With all the STRC doom loop FUD and people complaining about Saylor "forced selling" you'd expect MSTR investors to be more fearful than Bitcoiners right?

Nope.

Opposite actually.

This chart visualizes the fearful language of MSTR investors vs Bitcoiners.

It's interesting because it allows us to separate MSTR investor sentiment from the background emotional state of Bitcoin.

"But Sully, MSTR is a Bitcoin derivative, shouldn't the mood swings be more pronounced?"

This is often the case... but it's not the case right now.

There are a lot of potential reason for the widening psychological gap between investor bases (BIP-110, Coldard, etc). Regardless of the underlying reasons, the void is widening.

IMO this is one of the most fascinating dynamics in the space and basically no one is talking about it right now.

BREAKING: The Index of US Financial Conditions is up to ~1.29 points, the easiest since 1997.

This index measures access to money across financial markets, incorporating things like interest rates, credit spreads, stock prices, the dollar, and overall borrowing conditions.

By comparison, during the March 2026 market selloff, the index was on the verge of turning negative.

Not even during the 2021 meme stock frenzy were financial conditions this easy.

The latest surge has been driven by equity markets hitting all-time highs, with US corporate bond credit spreads remaining near their tightest levels since 1998.

Retail investors are piling into gold-mining stocks:

The gold miners ETF, $GDX, attracted +$9 million in retail inflows on Wednesday, posting its 6th daily inflow over the last 7 trading sessions.

This follows +$17 million recorded on Monday and +$25 million on Friday, the largest daily inflow in at least a year.

By comparison, the previous largest daily inflow in 2026 was +$23 million posted in February.

Overall, $GDX has attracted +$419 million in inflows so far this month, putting it on track for its largest monthly intake since February.

Demand for gold miners is skyrocketing.

Weakness in US full-time employment is deepening:

Full-time employment fell-106,000 in July, to 133.55 million, the lowest since December 2024.

This marks the 4th consecutive monthly decline, totaling -1.11 million. 

Since January 2025, full-time employment has dropped by -2.35 million

As a result, the number of full-time workers in the US is now just 1.4% above pre-pandemic levels.

Meanwhile, the full-time employment-to-total employment ratio has fallen to 82.4%, the 3rd-lowest level since March 2018.

US labor market is weak beneath the surface.

US tech is generating record gains for foreign institutional investors:

Norway’s $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, the world’s largest, generated a record +$184.3 billion in profit in H1 2026.

This comes as the fund returned +9.4% over the period, while its 72.1% equity allocation was up +13.0%.

In Q2 2026 alone, the portfolio gained +11.5%, its strongest quarterly performance since Q2 2020.

Equities, primarily driven by AI-related names, led the gains with a +16.0% return during the quarter.

Meanwhile, Nvidia, $NVDA, remained its largest holding at the end of H1 2026, followed by Microsoft, $MSFT, and Apple, $AAPL.

Norway’s fund owns ~1.5% of all publicly listed companies globally and has become one of the world’s largest institutional investors in AI-related companies.

The AI revolution is boosting investment portfolios far beyond America.

For bond investors the choice is always between nominal and real, and as shown in the Real vs. Nominal Yields chart, since 2021 TIPS have outperformed nominals. I expect that to continue as nominals seem too low given where the implied inflation expectations are.

Whether or not the TIPS break-evens carry a market signal (as is commonly assumed) remains an open question for me. Just like the oil futures strip, I’m not sure that break-evens reflect a conscious market opinion or are just a residual of two types of instruments. Case in point: the TIPS chart below shows the TIPS real yield along the horizontal and the break-even along the vertical. I don’t see a pattern between the two.

US-based investors are dumping Chinese equities:

US-listed China ETFs recorded -$3.4 billion in combined outflows across May, June, and July.

This includes the China Large-Cap ETF, $FXI, the MSCI China ETF, $MCHI, the CSI 300 China ETF, $ASHR, the China Internet ETF, $KWEB, the China Technology ETF, $CQQQ, and the China Technology and Semiconductor ETF, $KSTR.

As a result, the 12-month cumulative outflow fell to -$1.0 billion through July, the largest withdrawal in at least a year.

Year-to-date, the China Large-Cap ETF, $FXI, has seen the largest outflow at -$1.6 billion.

This is followed by the MSCI China ETF, $MCHI, at -$868 million, and the China Internet ETF, $KWEB, at -$833 million.

Investor demand for Chinese equities is weak.
